hints: Recall whether magnesium nitrate or barium nitrate needs stronger heating to decompose, to decide the direction of the stability trend down the group.
Compare the size of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and think about how charge density changes with increasing proton number.
Think about how a small highly charging cation distorts the $\text{NO}_3^-$ electron cloud and weakens an $\text{N-O}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Picture the trend in stability**
Think of heating $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$. The magnesium compound decomposes very easily while the barium compound needs much stronger heating. So stability increases going down the group as proton number increases.

Link stability to cation size**
All the cations are $2+$, but $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is very small and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is much larger. Charge density is charge divided by size, so it falls down the group. A small ion concentrates its $2+$ charge in a tiny volume.

See polarisation as the key action**
When the cation sits next to $\text{NO}_3^-$, its positive charge pulls on the electrons of the nitrate ion. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ distorts that electron cloud strongly, this is polarisation. It weakens one $\text{N-O}$ bond and makes it easy to break to give $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ polarises much less, so the nitrate stays more stable.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2 with increasing proton number.
Down the group the radius of $\text{M}^{2+}$ increases so charge density decreases.
The larger cation causes less polarisation / distortion of $\text{NO}_3^-$, so less weakening of the $\text{N-O}$ bond and more heat is needed to decompose it.

hints: Remember that nitrates of metals below Group 2 in polarising power decompose to the metal oxide plus nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.
walkthrough:
Use the Group 2 pattern**
Group 2 nitrates give metal oxide + nitrogen dioxide + oxygen: $2\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$. Copper(II) follows the same pattern because $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is small and polarising.

Balance for one formula unit**
One $\text{Cu}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ contains one Cu, two N and six O. Products $\text{CuO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$ also give Cu 1, N 2, O $1+4+1 = 6$. That balances atoms and charge.
Final answer: $\text{Cu}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{CuO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$

hints: Start with solution A formed when the nitrate salt simply dissolves, what ligand surrounds $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in dilute aqueous solution and what is its familiar pale colour?
Recall what happens when a small amount of $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ acts as a base toward $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ to give a pale blue precipitate.
Think about how excess ammonia and excess concentrated chloride each replace ligands by ligand exchange to give intensely coloured complexes.
Match each product to its classic Cambridge colour: pale blue solution, pale blue precipitate, dark blue solution, yellow solution.
walkthrough:
Identify solution A**
Dissolving $\text{Cu}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ in water gives the hexaaquacopper(II) ion. Water acts as the ligand: $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$. You know this as the familiar pale blue solution of copper(II) salts.

Identify precipitate B**
Adding a little $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ provides $\text{OH}^-$ from $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$. The hydroxide removes protons from coordinated water to precipitate copper(II) hydroxide: $\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2$, a pale blue precipitate.

Identify solution C with excess ammonia**
With excess $\text{NH}_3$, ammonia molecules replace water ligands by ligand exchange to form the tetraammine complex $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$. This is the unmistakable deep dark blue solution.

Identify solution D with excess concentrated HCl**
With excess concentrated $\text{Cl}^-$, chloride replaces all water ligands to give the tetrahedral complex $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$. This is yellow, often seen as yellow-green when mixed with some remaining blue species.

Final answer: A: $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ ; (pale) blue
B: $\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2$ or $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$ ; (pale) blue precipitate
C: $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ ; dark blue
D: $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$ ; yellow

hints: Break the word polydentate into poly meaning many and dentate meaning teeth that bite onto the metal.
Recall what type of bond every ligand forms to a metal ion and what the ligand must supply to form it.
walkthrough:
Understand dentate**
Monodentate like $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{NH}_3$ uses one atom to donate one lone pair. Bidentate like 1,2-diaminoethane uses two atoms. Poly means many, so polydentate means more than two donor atoms.

Add the bonding detail**
Each donor atom supplies a lone pair into an empty orbital on the metal to make a dative covalent or coordinate bond. So a polydentate ligand forms more than two such bonds to the same metal ion, wrapping around it like a claw.

Final answer: A ligand that donates more than two lone pairs of electrons
to form dative / coordinate bonds to a (central) metal atom or ion.

hints: Count the donor atoms needed for coordination number 6 and look for nitrogen atoms with lone pairs and negatively charged oxygen atoms in carboxylate groups.
walkthrough:
Spot the donors in EDTA**
Look at Fig. 1.2. The two central N atoms each have a lone pair. Each of the four $\text{-CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$ arms has a $\text{C=O}$ and a $\text{C-O}^-$. Only the $\text{O}^-$ oxygen with the negative charge donates its lone pair, not the $\text{C=O}$ oxygen. That gives $2 + 4 = 6$ donor atoms, so EDTA is hexadentate.
Final answer: Circle the two N atoms and the four singly bonded $\text{O}^-$ atoms, one from each $\text{CO}_2^-$ group (total six atoms, $2\text{N} + 4\text{O}$).

hints: Think about counting bonds from the metal's point of view, not counting ligands but counting attachments.
walkthrough:
Define from the metal centre**
Coordination number tells you how many donor atoms are directly attached to the metal. Each attachment is a coordinate bond where the ligand donates a pair. Here both $\text{[Ca(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ with six waters and $\text{[CaEDTA]}^{2-}$ with six donor atoms have coordination number 6.
Final answer: The number of coordinate / dative bonds formed to the metal ion.

hints: Notice that EDTA replaces water around calcium and that other metal ions can later replace calcium, so one ligand is swapping for another.
walkthrough:
Recognise the reaction type**
In equilibrium 1, six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are swapped for one $\text{EDTA}^{4-}$. Later $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ or $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ displace $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ from $\text{[CaEDTA]}^{2-}$. Whenever one ligand replaces another in the coordination sphere, chemists call it ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand substitution.
Final answer: Ligand exchange / ligand substitution

hints: Compare the $K_{stab}$ values in Table 1.2 and remember that a larger $K_{stab}$ means a more stable complex and an equilibrium lying further to the right.
walkthrough:
Use Kstab to predict**
$K_{stab}$ measures how strongly the complex holds together. Table 1.2 gives $1.3 \times 10^{25}$ for Fe, $2.5 \times 10^{23}$ for Cr, $1.1 \times 10^{18}$ for Pb. The largest value means the Fe equilibrium lies furthest to the right, so most EDTA ends up bound to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, then $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, with least bound to $\text{Pb}^{2+}$.

Final answer: $\text{[FeEDTA]}^-$ (highest concentration) > $\text{[CrEDTA]}^-$ > $\text{[PbEDTA]}^{2-}$ (lowest concentration) because $K_{stab}$ of $\text{[FeEDTA]}^-$ is highest ($1.3 \times 10^{25}$).

hints: Start from the titration figures to find moles of $\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ used in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$, which equals moles of $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ in that aliquot from the 1:1 equation.

Scale up from $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ to the full $100 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, then use the $2:1$ ratio of $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ to $\text{Cr}_2\text{(SO}_4\text{)}_3 \cdot n\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to find moles of hydrated salt.
Use mass divided by moles to get $M_r$ of the hydrated salt, subtract $M_r$ of anhydrous $\text{Cr}_2\text{(SO}_4\text{)}_3$ and divide by 18 to find $n$.
walkthrough:
Find moles in the titration aliquot**
Moles = concentration times volume in $\text{dm}^3$. $$n(\text{EDTA}^{4-}) = 0.00800 \times \frac{26.2}{1000} = 2.096 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$ The equation shows 1 $\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ reacts with 1 $\text{[Cr(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{3+}$, so this is also moles of $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$.

Scale to the whole sample**
The flask holds $100 \text{ cm}^3$, four times the aliquot: $$n(\text{Cr}^{3+}\text{ total}) = 2.096 \times 10^{-4} \times 4 = 8.384 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$ Each $\text{Cr}_2\text{(SO}_4\text{)}_3 \cdot n\text{H}_2\text{O}$ supplies two $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, so: $$n(\text{salt}) = \frac{8.384 \times 10^{-4}}{2} = 4.192 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

Convert to Mr and extract n**
$$M_r(\text{hydrated salt}) = \frac{0.2550}{4.192 \times 10^{-4}} = 608.3$$ Anhydrous $M_r = 2(52.0) + 3(32.1+64.0) = 392.3$. Mass due to water $= 608.3 - 392.3 = 216.0$. $$n = \frac{216.0}{18.0} = 12$$ So the formula is $\text{Cr}_2\text{(SO}_4\text{)}_3 \cdot 12\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Remember that colour in transition metal complexes comes from splitting of d orbitals and promotion of an electron between the split levels.
Think about why $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ would split the d orbitals by a different amount and what that means for the light absorbed.
walkthrough:
Recall where colour comes from**
In $\text{[Cr(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{3+}$ and $\text{[Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{3+}$ the ligands split the 3d orbitals into two sets separated by $\Delta E$. White light shines in, an electron absorbs a photon with energy equal to $\Delta E$ and jumps up. The colour you see is the rest of the light that is not absorbed.

Explain the difference**
$\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^3$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^5$, with different nuclear charge and d electron repulsion. So the size of the splitting $\Delta E$ is different. That means a different frequency of light is absorbed in each case, leaving a different complementary colour to reach your eye.

Final answer: The d-orbital splitting / $\Delta E$ is different in the two complexes.
A different frequency / wavelength / energy of (visible) light is absorbed to promote a d electron, so different colours are transmitted / observed.
